headline: Family is defined by bonds, not biology—chosen connections can be as powerful as blood
universal_truth: Belonging is a fundamental need that can be met in many ways
fun_facts: The concept of 'nuclear family' is historically recent—extended families were the norm for most of human history
Children raised in loving environments thrive regardless of family structure
Many cultures consider close friends as family—language often has words for 'chosen siblings'
discussion_questions: Who do you consider family beyond blood relatives?
How has your definition of family changed over time?
What makes a bond feel like family?

hook.script: The word 'family' might conjure parents and siblings. But look closer: family is really about connection, support, and belonging. Adopted children, chosen friends, created communities—family is defined by bonds, not just biology.

cliff.script: If family can mean many things, what actually makes a family? Is it shared DNA? Living together? Legal ties? Or something harder to define but easier to feel?

options.text: Mutual commitment, support, and a sense of belonging—regardless of biology
options.response: Yes. Research shows that love, commitment, and stability matter more than family structure.

options.text: Shared genetics and legal relationships form the foundation
options.response: These can create family, but many families exist without them...

fact1.title: Recent Invention
fact1.script: The 'nuclear family'—two parents and their children, living alone—is historically unusual. For most of human history, extended families, multigenerational households, and community-raising of children was normal. Our current model is the exception.

fact2.title: What Matters
fact2.script: Decades of research show that children thrive based on love, stability, and support—not family structure. Single parents, same-sex parents, grandparents, adopted families—the form matters less than the function.

fact3.title: Chosen Family
fact3.script: Many cultures recognize 'chosen family'—bonds as strong as blood, formed through choice and commitment. These relationships can provide the same psychological benefits as biological family. You can build family as well as inherit it.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Belonging is a need, and family is how we meet it. But the form is flexible. You can receive family, create family, and choose family. What matters is the connection, not the category.

outro.script: That's Day 91—welcome to April's Mind & Skills month! Tomorrow, we'll explore how we understand each other. Until then, appreciate the family you have—however you define it.

growTrack.title: Family Inventory - Who Belongs to You?
growTrack.learning_objective: Recognize and appreciate your actual support network
growTrack.activity: Make a list of your 'family'—not just blood relatives, but everyone who provides you belonging, support, and connection. Who shows up for you? Who do you show up for? This is your real family, whatever the labels.
